chapters.name: Chapter 1: How AI is changing work

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Where AI shows up at work today
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 4 minutes
Goal: Name three ways AI is already used in jobs around you.
This lesson builds toward: Given a job you or your family know, you will identify tasks AI can help with and tasks a person still needs to do, naming at least two of each.
AI is computer software that can do tasks that usually need a person, like writing, sorting, answering questions or spotting patterns. You may already see it every day.
At a store, AI helps decide how much stock to order. At a call center, a chatbot answers simple questions before a person takes over. In a clinic, software helps write visit notes. In a warehouse, scanners and robots help track boxes.
In most jobs, AI does not replace the whole job. It takes over some tasks, and people do the rest: talking with customers, solving problems, fixing things, caring for others and making decisions.
Words to know:
- AI: short for artificial intelligence: software that does tasks that usually need a person.
- Task: one piece of a job, like answering the phone or counting stock.
Try it now: Think of a job you or a family member has had. Write down two tasks AI could help with and two tasks a person still needs to do.
You can now name ways AI is used at work and explain why people are still needed.

options: Software that does tasks that usually need a person
A robot that does every job
check.why: AI is software that can write, sort, answer questions or spot patterns.

check.q: In a clinic, software writes visit notes. Which task does a person still do?
options: Typing every word of the notes
Comforting and caring for the patient
Nothing; the software does it all
check.why: AI takes some tasks, but people still care for others and make decisions.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Growing jobs and the skills they need
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Find a growing job and its pay on the official Occupational Outlook Handbook.
This lesson builds toward: Using the Occupational Outlook Handbook at bls.gov/ooh, you will find a growing job and write down its median pay, training and job outlook, from the current page.
Some jobs are growing because of technology, and some are growing because people will always need them, like health care, skilled trades and caring for children and older adults.
The U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics runs a free website called the Occupational Outlook Handbook at bls.gov/ooh. For hundreds of jobs it tells you what the work is, the usual pay, the training needed and how fast the job is expected to grow.
For example, the Handbook expects computer and information technology jobs as a group to grow faster than average from 2025 to 2035. Numbers like these are updated, so always read the current page yourself.
Step by step:
- Go to bls.gov/ooh on a phone or library computer.
- Choose a job group, such as Healthcare or Computer and Information Technology.
- Click one job.
- Write down the pay, the training needed and the job outlook.
Words to know:
- Job outlook: how fast the number of jobs is expected to grow or shrink.
- Median pay: the middle pay: half the workers earn more and half earn less.
Official sources:
- U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics: Occupational Outlook Handbook, Computer and Information Technology
Try it now: Open bls.gov/ooh, pick one job that interests you, and write down its median pay, the training it needs and its job outlook.
You can now look up any job on the official Occupational Outlook Handbook and read its pay, training and outlook.

check.q: Who runs the Occupational Outlook Handbook?
options: The U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics
check.why: The Handbook at bls.gov/ooh is run by the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics.

check.q: A friend tells you a job's pay from a page they saved years ago. What do you do?
options: Ask the AI to confirm it
Read the current page on bls.gov/ooh
check.why: Pay and outlook numbers are updated, so you read the current page yourself.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Using AI to explore a job
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Ask a free AI assistant clear questions about a job, then check the answers.
This lesson builds toward: Using a free AI assistant, you will ask clear questions about a job's daily work and skills, then check pay, license and training facts on official sites, with no private details in the prompt.
A free AI assistant such as ChatGPT, Microsoft Copilot or Google Gemini can explain a job in simple words, list the skills it needs and suggest questions to ask people who do it.
Give it your situation without private details. For example: "I have worked in fast food for 3 years and I like helping people. Explain what a medical assistant does in a normal day, in simple words."
AI can be wrong about pay, licenses and training. Check those facts on bls.gov/ooh or your state's official site before you make plans.
Step by step:
- Open a free AI assistant.
- Tell it the job and a little about your experience.
- Ask what a normal day looks like and what skills it needs.
- Check pay and training on bls.gov/ooh.
Words to know:
- Prompt: what you type or say to an AI assistant.
- License: official permission from the state to do certain jobs.
Try it now: Ask an AI assistant to explain your chosen job's normal day and its top five skills. Compare one fact with what bls.gov/ooh says.
You can now use AI to learn about a job and check its facts on an official site.

check.q: Which facts from an AI must you check on official sites?
options: How to spell the job name
check.why: AI can be wrong about pay, licenses and training, so you check them.

check.q: You want AI to explain a warehouse supervisor job. What do you include?
options: Your experience and what you like, without private details
check.why: Your experience helps the AI explain the job for you; private details stay out.

chapters.name: Chapter 2: Getting ready for your next step

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Finding free training near you
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Find two free or low-cost places to learn the skills for your job.
This lesson builds toward: Given the skills a job needs, you will find two free or low-cost places near you to learn them, writing down each name, phone number and hours.
You do not need a lot of money to start learning. Public libraries often offer free computer classes and free online learning. Community colleges offer low-cost certificates, and many students qualify for financial aid.
American Job Centers are run with the U.S. Department of Labor. They help with job search, job referrals and training. Some services have eligibility rules, so ask your local center what you qualify for. Find one with the CareerOneStop American Job Center Finder or call 1-877-US-2JOBS.
Ask a free AI assistant: "What free ways can I learn basic skills for a medical assistant job?" Then check each idea with the library, college or job center itself.
Step by step:
- Ask your library what free classes and online learning it offers.
- Look up the nearest community college and its certificate programs.
- Find your nearest American Job Center with the CareerOneStop finder.
- Write down two places, their phone numbers and their hours.
Words to know:
- Certificate: a short training program that proves you learned a job skill.
- American Job Center: a local office, run with the U.S. Department of Labor, that helps people find jobs and training.
Official sources:
- U.S. Department of Labor: American Job Centers
- CareerOneStop: American Job Center Finder
Try it now: Find two places near you where you could learn skills for your job. Write down each name, phone number and hours.
You can now find free or low-cost training near you for the job you want.

check.q: What do community colleges often offer?
options: Low-cost certificates, with financial aid for many students
check.why: Community colleges offer low-cost certificates, and many students qualify for aid.

check.q: You are not sure if you qualify for training at an American Job Center. What do you do?
options: Pay a website to find out
Ask your local center what you qualify for
check.why: Some services have eligibility rules, so you ask the center directly.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Turning a goal into small steps
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 4 minutes
Goal: Break a job goal into three small steps with dates.
This lesson builds toward: Given a job goal, you will create a one-page plan with three small steps and a date for each, each step doable in a week or two and fitted to your time and family.
A big goal like "get a better job" can feel too large. Small steps with dates make it real.
A good step is something you can finish in a week or two: "Call the library on Tuesday to sign up for the computer class." "Talk to one person who works as a medical assistant by the 15th."
You can ask an AI assistant to help: "Help me break my goal of becoming a medical assistant into three small steps for the next month. I can spend 3 hours a week." Then change the plan so it fits your life, your family and your schedule.
Step by step:
- Write your goal in one sentence.
- Ask AI to break it into three small steps.
- Give each step a date.
- Change the plan to fit your time and family.
Words to know:
- Goal: something you want to reach.
- Deadline: the date you plan to finish a step.
Try it now: Write your job goal in one sentence. Ask an AI assistant to break it into three steps for the next month, then add a date to each step.
You can now turn a job goal into three small steps with dates.

check.q: Which is a small step you can finish in a week or two?
options: Talk to one medical assistant by the 15th
check.why: A small step is specific, doable soon and has a date.

check.q: The AI's plan says to study 10 hours a week, but you have 3. What do you do?
options: Change the plan to fit your time
Ask the AI to study for you
check.why: You change the plan so it fits your life, your family and your schedule.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Your plan, and staying safe while you look
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Finish your one-page plan and spot fake job and training offers.
This lesson builds toward: Given a job or training offer, you will check it for scam warning signs and keep private numbers out, before you pay, sign or share anything. Given a job goal, you will create a one-page plan with three small steps and a date for each, each step doable in a week or two and fitted to your time and family.
Put it all together on one page: the job, its pay and outlook from bls.gov/ooh, two skills you need, two places to learn, and three dated steps. Keep it on your phone or print it at the library.
Be careful. Scammers post fake jobs and fake training. Warning signs: they ask you to pay to get the job, ask for your bank or Social Security number before an interview, promise high pay for little work, or rush you.
Never type your Social Security number, bank details or passwords into an AI assistant. Check any training program with your library, job center or the school's official website before you pay or sign anything.
Step by step:
- Write the job, pay and outlook.
- Add two skills and two places to learn.
- Add your three dated steps.
- Check every offer for scam warning signs before you share anything.
Words to know:
- Scam: a trick to steal money or information.
Try it now: Final task: write your one-page plan with the job, pay and outlook, two skills, two places to learn and three dated steps. Check it for anything private before you share it.
You can now make a real, checked plan for a growing job and avoid common job scams.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Job facts Pay or outlook is missing or not from bls.gov/ooh. The job, what it is, its pay and outlook, checked on the current bls.gov/ooh page. Also lists the training the job needs. Skills No skills, or skills that do not fit the job. Two skills the job needs. Notes which skill the learner already has from past work. Places to learn Fewer than two places, or no contact details. Two free or low-cost places with name, phone and hours. Notes what each place offers and any eligibility to ask about. Three dated steps Steps are vague or have no dates. Three small steps for the next month, each with a date. Fitted to the learner's real time and family schedule. Safe to share The plan has a private number, or a training offer was not checked. No private numbers, and offers checked for warning signs. Can name the warning signs they looked for. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: Which is a warning sign of a fake job?
options: An interview at the company's office
A posting on the company's own website
A rush to pay before you can be hired
A job listed by your American Job Center
check.why: Real employers do not ask you to pay to get the job or rush you.

check.q: A training school online wants payment today for a "guaranteed job". What do you do?
options: Pay today to save your spot
Check it with the school's official site, your library or job center
check.why: Check any training program with trusted sources before you pay or sign.
